For a buyer the practical points are the form bought, the basis a result is reported on, where the chicken came from and the laboratory’s reporting limit. Testing finds contamination but does not remove it.



<a id="ingredient-identity-and-scope"></a>
## What counts as chicken

<a id="hmi-ing-001"></a>
<a id="what-commodity-biological-species-edible-part-and-commercial-forms-does-this-page-cover"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-002"></a>
<a id="which-processing-states-and-derivatives-are-distinct-materials-rather-than-synonyms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-003"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-can-be-transferred-between-those-materials-and-what-requires-a-separate-answer"></a>

This page covers chicken in 6 forms kept separate in every comparison: chicken, as sold (1,726 results), chicken, cooked (153 results), chicken, frozen (54 results), chicken, canned (37 results), chicken, powder or ground (20 results) and chicken, peeled or flesh (4 results).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span <div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-chicken" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-chicken-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of chicken, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>77</td><td>50%</td></tr><tr><td>Henríquez-Hernández et al. 2023</td><td>2</td><td>50%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for chicken, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>2 sampling families with different designs; none is a probability sample of world supply. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. A position is descriptive concentration, not a safety or compliance judgment.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Admitted source families</p><ul><li><a href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" class="internal" data-slug="sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" data-no-cite-meta>WHO GEMS/Food</a></li><li><a href="../sources/henriquez-hernandez2023-baby-purees-spain-elements" class="internal" data-slug="sources/henriquez-hernandez2023-baby-purees-spain-elements" data-no-cite-meta>Henríquez-Hernández et al. 2023</a></li></ul><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Reference version and interpretation</summary><p>Frozen evidence selection: 2026-10-22. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach chicken

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach chicken comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Chicken, as sold from conventional factory feed, floor housing (1st control group) (experiment) had lead higher at 24.7 µg/kg, against 3.53 µg/kg for conventional factory feed, cage housing (2nd control group) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/lysenko2021-organic-broiler-meat-heavy-metals|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Lysenko Y, Koshchayev A, Luneva A, Omarov R, Shlykov S · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/lysenko2021-organic-broiler-meat-heavy-metals">Organic Meat Production of Broiler Chickens Hubbard Redbro Cross</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Veterinary Science 10(1):62-68</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/lysenko2021-organic-broiler-meat-heavy-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, chicken, as sold from household-kept hens, tissue content (Table 3) (experiment) had Cu higher at 4,600 µg/kg, against 910 µg/kg for control group, main diet (Table 6) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/razanov2019-poultry-silicon-mineral-heavy-metals|22]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Razanov SF, Hutsol GV, Posternak LI, Kovaleva SP · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/razanov2019-poultry-silicon-mineral-heavy-metals">Effect of silicon and mineral extract on heavy metals balance and accumulation rate in the muscle tissue of poultry</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Ukrainian Journal of Ecology 9(4):742-748</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/razanov2019-poultry-silicon-mineral-heavy-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> A third study found that chicken, as sold from frozen drumstick, grocery shops, Umuahia had cadmium higher at 94 µg/kg, against 19 µg/kg for fresh drumstick, poultry farms around Umuahia in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/okolo2022-chicken-drumstick-umuhia-heavy-metals|23]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Okolo JC, Igborgbor JC, Anana UE, Ogu GI · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/okolo2022-chicken-drumstick-umuhia-heavy-metals">Chemical and microbiological quality of commercial fresh and frozen chicken drumstick in Umuhia, Nigeria</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Food, Agriculture, and Natural Resources</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/okolo2022-chicken-drumstick-umuhia-heavy-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-chicken" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-chicken" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in chicken?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in chicken?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, chicken, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (7.3 µg/kg) and the highest in WPRO (448 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in EURO (1.31 µg/kg) and the highest in EMRO (24 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-chicken" data-anchor="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-chicken" data-question="Does processing change heavy metals in chicken?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does processing change heavy metals in chicken?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Only comparisons between forms in the same study are available, not before-and-after measurements of the same chicken.<sup class="cite">[[sources/jayanthi2019-chennai-chicken-heavy-metals|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">R. Jayanthi, V. Appa Rao, R. Narendra Babu, T. Sivakumar, P. Sriram, Robinson J. J. Abraham · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/jayanthi2019-chennai-chicken-heavy-metals">Assessment of non-essential heavy metals in ready-to-eat chicken meat products of Chennai city</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Chemical Studies</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/jayanthi2019-chennai-chicken-heavy-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Chicken, cooked (central Chennai (street food outlets)) had lead higher at 960 µg/kg, against 600 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (chicken, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/jayanthi2019-chennai-chicken-heavy-metals|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">R. Jayanthi, V. Appa Rao, R. Narendra Babu, T. Sivakumar, P. Sriram, Robinson J. J. Abraham · 2019</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/jayanthi2019-chennai-chicken-heavy-metals">Assessment of non-essential heavy metals in ready-to-eat chicken meat products of Chennai city</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Chemical Studies</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/jayanthi2019-chennai-chicken-heavy-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>
